title: Controlling Severe Bleeding
summary: How to stop life-threatening blood loss using direct pressure and tourniquets.
contentMarkdown:
## Controlling Severe Bleeding

### Step 1 — Call for Help
If possible, call emergency services **before** starting treatment.

### Step 2 — Apply Direct Pressure
- Use a clean cloth, bandage, or any available fabric.
- Press **firmly** on the wound — do not lift to check.
- Maintain pressure for at least **10 minutes**.

### Step 3 — Tourniquet (Limb Only)
If bleeding does not stop and the wound is on an arm or leg:
1. Apply tourniquet **5–7 cm above** the wound (not on a joint).
2. Tighten until bleeding stops.
3. **Write the time applied** on the skin with a pen.
4. Never remove a tourniquet in the field.

### Step 4 — Keep the Person Calm
- Lay the person down.
- Elevate the injured limb if no fracture is suspected.
- Keep them warm to prevent shock.

> **Warning**: Do not remove embedded objects. Pack gauze around them.

### Signs of Shock to Watch For
- Pale, cold, or clammy skin
- Rapid, weak pulse
- Confusion or loss of consciousness

title: Treating Burns
summary: Immediate actions for minor and major burn injuries.
contentMarkdown:
## Treating Burns

### Classify the Burn
| Degree | Appearance | Action |
|--------|------------|--------|
| 1st | Red, no blisters | Cool water, no creams |
| 2nd | Blisters, swelling | Cool water, loose dressing |
| 3rd | White/charred | Seek immediate care |

### For Minor Burns (1st & 2nd Degree)
1. **Cool** the burn under clean running water for **10–20 minutes**.
2. **Do NOT** use ice, butter, toothpaste, or oils.
3. Cover loosely with a **non-fluffy sterile dressing**.
4. Take a pain reliever if available.

### For Major Burns (3rd Degree / Large Area)
- Do **not** remove burned clothing stuck to skin.
- Cover with a clean, moist cloth.
- Treat for shock (keep warm, lay down, raise legs).
- Get to medical care as fast as possible.

### What to Avoid
- Breaking blisters
- Applying any household remedies
- Tight bandages

title: Shelter-In-Place Protocol
summary: How to safely shelter inside a building during an attack or chemical hazard.
contentMarkdown:
## Shelter-In-Place Protocol

### When to Shelter In Place
- Active artillery or air strike nearby
- Chemical or biological hazard outside
- Authorities issue a shelter-in-place order

### Choose Your Room
- An **interior room** above ground level (not basement if flooding risk).
- Fewest windows and doors.
- Ideally above the flood plain.

### Seal the Room
1. Close all windows and doors.
2. Use **duct tape and plastic sheeting** to seal gaps around doors, windows, and vents.
3. Seal fireplace dampers and exhaust fans.

### Supplies to Have Ready
- Water (at least 4 litres per person per day)
- Food for 72 hours
- Battery-powered or hand-crank radio
- First aid kit
- Flashlight with extra batteries
- Medications

### While Sheltered
- Keep a battery-powered radio tuned to emergency broadcasts.
- Check on other household members regularly.
- Limit phone use to preserve battery.

### When to Leave
- Follow official instructions only.
- Ventilate the room for a few minutes before leaving if a chemical event is suspected.

title: 72-Hour Go-Bag Checklist
summary: Everything you need in a bug-out bag to survive 72 hours on the move.
contentMarkdown:
## 72-Hour Go-Bag Checklist

Pack your bag in advance. Refresh water and food every 6 months.

### Water & Food
- [ ] 2 litres of water per person
- [ ] Water purification tablets
- [ ] High-energy non-perishable food (energy bars, canned goods)
- [ ] Manual can opener

### Documents & Money
- [ ] Photocopies of ID, passport, insurance cards
- [ ] Small amount of cash (cards may not work)
- [ ] USB drive with digital copies of documents

### First Aid
- [ ] Pre-stocked first aid kit
- [ ] 7-day supply of prescription medications
- [ ] Glasses / contact lenses + solution

### Tools & Safety
- [ ] Flashlight + extra batteries
- [ ] Multi-tool or pocket knife
- [ ] Whistle (signal for help)
- [ ] Dust masks (N95 or better)
- [ ] Waterproof matches or lighter
- [ ] Emergency blanket (Mylar)

### Communication
- [ ] Battery-powered or hand-crank radio
- [ ] Fully charged mobile phone + portable charger
- [ ] Written list of key phone numbers

### Clothing
- [ ] One change of clothes per person
- [ ] Sturdy, closed-toe shoes
- [ ] Rain poncho

### Special Needs
- [ ] Infant formula / diapers (if needed)
- [ ] Pet food (if applicable)
- [ ] Comfort item for children

title: Emergency Water Purification
summary: Safe methods to make water drinkable without electricity or specialty equipment.
contentMarkdown:
## Emergency Water Purification

> **Rule**: When in doubt, purify it.

### Method 1 — Boiling (Most Reliable)
1. Bring water to a **rolling boil** for at least **1 minute**.
2. At altitudes above 2,000 m: boil for **3 minutes**.
3. Let cool and store in a clean covered container.

### Method 2 — Chemical Disinfection
**Unscented household bleach (5–8% chlorine)**:
- Clear water: **8 drops per litre**
- Cloudy water: **16 drops per litre**
- Stir, wait **30 minutes** before drinking.

**Water purification tablets**:
- Follow manufacturer's instructions.
- Usually 1 tablet per litre; wait 30 minutes.

### Method 3 — Solar Disinfection (SODIS)
1. Fill a clear PET plastic bottle with filtered water.
2. Place in direct sunlight for **6 hours** (or 2 days if cloudy).
3. Effective against bacteria and viruses.

### Pre-treating Cloudy Water
- Filter through a cloth, coffee filter, or sand/gravel layers first.
- This removes sediment and improves disinfection effectiveness.

### Storage
- Use clean, covered containers.
- Do not touch the inside of the container.
- Store away from sunlight and heat.

title: CPR — Basic Life Support
summary: Step-by-step hands-only and full CPR for adults.
contentMarkdown:
## CPR — Basic Life Support

### Check Scene Safety First
Do not approach if the area is unsafe (fire, unstable structure, etc.).

### Check the Person
1. Tap the shoulder firmly: **"Are you okay?"**
2. If no response → Call emergency services immediately.

### Hands-Only CPR (Untrained)
1. Place heel of one hand on the **centre of the chest**.
2. Place other hand on top, interlace fingers.
3. Push **hard and fast** — at least **5 cm deep** at **100–120 beats/minute** (roughly the beat of *Stayin' Alive*).
4. Do not stop until help arrives or the person recovers.

### Full CPR (Trained)
- **30 chest compressions** → **2 rescue breaths**
- Tilt head back, lift chin, pinch nose, seal mouth, breathe for 1 second.
- Repeat cycle.

### Using an AED (If Available)
1. Turn on the AED and follow voice prompts.
2. Attach pads as shown on the diagrams.
3. Clear everyone → press shock button if advised.
4. Resume CPR immediately after shock.

### For Children (1–8 years)
- Use **one or two hands** depending on child's size.
- Compress **4 cm deep**.
- Use gentle rescue breaths.

### Stop CPR If
- Scene becomes unsafe
- Person shows clear signs of life
- AED is ready to analyse
- Professional responders take over

title: Build a Bottle Water Pre-Filter
summary: Make a quick pre-filter from cloth, charcoal, sand, and gravel before boiling or disinfecting.
contentMarkdown:
## Build a Bottle Water Pre-Filter

> **Important**: This removes sediment and some bad taste. It does **not** make water safe on its own. Always boil or disinfect afterward.

### What You Need
- Plastic bottle or cut container
- Clean cloth
- Crushed charcoal from a clean wood fire
- Sand
- Small gravel or pebbles
- Second clean container

### Assembly
1. Cut the bottom off the bottle.
2. Put cloth in the neck so material cannot fall through.
3. Add layers from bottom to top: **cloth → charcoal → sand → gravel**.
4. Pour cloudy water in slowly.
5. Catch the filtered water in a clean container.
6. Run it through again if still dirty.

### Finish the Job
- **Boil** the filtered water for at least 1 minute.
- Or use bleach / purification tablets if available.

### Field Notes
- Replace the charcoal and cloth if the filter smells bad.
- Keep the clean container separate from dirty tools.
- Do not use charcoal from painted, treated, or plastic-contaminated materials.

title: Build a Debris Shelter from Scratch
summary: A low-tool shelter that traps body heat using branches, leaves, and dry debris.
contentMarkdown:
## Build a Debris Shelter from Scratch

### Choose the Site
- Pick ground above runoff and away from dead branches.
- Face the opening away from wind.
- Avoid riverbanks that can flood overnight.

### Frame
1. Find a strong ridge pole about as long as your body.
2. Lean it on a stump, rock, or forked branch.
3. Add ribs along both sides using smaller branches.
4. Keep the shelter just big enough for you to crawl into.

### Insulate
- Pile **dry leaves, grass, pine needles, or reeds** over the frame.
- Aim for at least **arm-thick insulation** on top.
- Add a deep layer of debris inside so you are not lying on bare ground.

### Door
- Use a jacket, bag, branches, or bundled grass to block the entrance.
- Leave a small gap for air.

### Field Notes
- Insulation underneath matters as much as the roof.
- Smaller shelter = warmer shelter.
- Replace wet debris quickly; wet insulation loses heat fast.

title: Make a Simple Twig Stove
summary: Create a compact cooking fire from scrap metal cans when fuel is limited.
contentMarkdown:
## Make a Simple Twig Stove

> **Warning**: Only use outdoors on bare soil or stone. Scrap metal edges are sharp and fire can spread quickly.

### What You Need
- 1 large metal can
- 1 smaller metal can or inner sleeve (optional)
- Can opener, nail, or punch tool
- Dry pencil-thin sticks

### Build
1. Punch air holes around the lower edge of the large can.
2. Cut a thumb-sized feed opening near the base.
3. If you have a second can, place it inside to create a narrow burn chamber.
4. Rest a pot above the opening using tent pegs, wire, or three stones.

### Use
- Start with dry tinder.
- Feed small sticks slowly through the side opening.
- Keep flames short and controlled.
- Boil water or heat food with the smallest fire that works.

### Safety
- Keep water or dirt nearby to kill the fire.
- Never use indoors or in a sealed shelter.
- Let the can cool fully before moving it.

title: Twist Emergency Cordage from Plant Fibers
summary: Make usable cord from bark, grass, fabric strips, or plastic bags.
contentMarkdown:
## Twist Emergency Cordage from Plant Fibers

### Good Materials
- Inner bark from flexible plants
- Long grass or reeds
- Torn cloth strips
- Plastic bag strips for water-resistant cord

### Two-Ply Method
1. Split material into two bundles.
2. Twist the first bundle away from you.
3. Cross it over the second bundle.
4. Twist the new outside bundle away from you.
5. Cross again.
6. Repeat until you have a cord.

### Strength Tips
- Keep tension constant.
- Add new fibers before the old ones end.
- Reverse-wrap a second finished cord with another for extra strength.

### Good Uses
- Shelter lashings
- Gear repair
- Splints
- Hanging food or wet clothing

### Do Not Use For
- Climbing
- Lifeline rescue loads
- Heavy towing

title: Emergency Phone Charging Without Grid Power
summary: Safe fallback options for keeping a phone alive when mains power is gone.
contentMarkdown:
## Emergency Phone Charging Without Grid Power

### Best Options First
1. Use a charged power bank.
2. Use a vehicle USB outlet or 12V adapter.
3. Use a solar panel **with a USB regulator or power bank in between**.
4. Use a hand-crank radio or emergency generator with USB output.

### Salvage Rules
- Prefer **devices that already output USB 5V**.
- Use the phone's normal cable whenever possible.
- Charge the phone while switched off or in airplane mode.
- Warm the phone in cold weather before charging.

### If You Salvage Battery Cells
- Do **not** connect loose wires directly to your phone.
- Do **not** charge from homemade lemon, saltwater, or coin cells; they are too weak and unstable for modern phones.
- Do **not** short lithium cells, puncture them, or combine random batteries.
- Only use scavenged cells with a proper charger board / regulated USB module if you know exactly what you are doing.

### Battery-Saving Wins
- Airplane mode on
- Screen brightness near minimum
- Battery saver on
- GPS, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi off unless needed
- Download maps and messages before power is low

title: Build a Ground Signal Marker
summary: Use rocks, cloth, branches, or scrap to make rescue signals visible from far away.
contentMarkdown:
## Build a Ground Signal Marker

### Best Shapes
- **SOS**
- Large **X** for assistance needed
- Straight arrow toward your shelter or route

### Materials
- Stones
- Logs or branches
- Bright cloth
- Reflective foil, mirrors, or metal sheet scraps

### Build Method
1. Choose open ground with maximum contrast.
2. Make each line at least **body-length wide** if you can.
3. Use straight edges and clean spacing.
4. Anchor cloth so wind cannot move it.
5. Add reflective material where sunlight may hit it.

### Improve Visibility
- Place next to open fields, roads, shorelines, or rooftops.
- Refresh after wind or rain.
- Pair with three whistle blasts or three fire/smoke signals when aircraft or rescuers are nearby.

### Avoid
- Small symbols only visible from nearby
- Building near flammable brush if using smoke signals
- Blocking your own escape route
